title: "The heat equation in real and Fourier space"

## Fourier's view: every mode on its own

Consider the heat (diffusion) equation on a periodic interval of length $L$,

$$
\psi_t = \nu\,\psi_{xx}.
$$ {#eq-heat}

Expand $\psi(x,t) = \sum_k \hat\psi_k(t)\, e^{ikx}$ with $k = 2\pi n/L$.
Because the equation is linear with constant coefficients, each mode evolves
independently:

$$
\frac{d\hat\psi_k}{dt} = -\nu k^2 \hat\psi_k
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\hat\psi_k(t) = \hat\psi_k(0)\, e^{-\nu k^2 t}.
$$ {#eq-heat-fourier}

This is the whole solution. There is no time stepping, no stability
constraint, no accumulation of error: one forward transform, a
multiplication by the **Fourier multiplier** $e^{-\nu k^2 t}$, one inverse
transform. Short wavelengths (large $k$) die first, which is why diffusion
smooths. After a time $t$ only modes with $k \lesssim (\nu t)^{-1/2}$ survive;
$\ell_{\rm diff} = \sqrt{\nu t}$ is the **diffusion length**.

## The real-space view: a kernel

The same solution can be written without any mention of Fourier modes. On the
infinite line the solution with a delta-function initial condition is the
**heat kernel**{{< src hopfcole::log_heat_convolve >}}

$$
G_t(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi\nu t}}\, e^{-x^2/4\nu t},
$$ {#eq-heat-kernel}

a Gaussian of variance $2\nu t$ and unit integral. By linearity the solution
for any initial condition is the superposition

$$
\psi(x,t) = \int G_t(x-y)\,\psi_0(y)\,dy = (G_t * \psi_0)(x).
$$ {#eq-heat-conv}

On a periodic domain the kernel is the periodic image sum
$\sum_m G_t(x + mL)$, and for $t > 0$ the solution is infinitely smooth no
matter how rough $\psi_0$ was.

::: {.callout-important title="One solution, two descriptions"}
@eq-heat-fourier and @eq-heat-conv are the *same* statement. The convolution
theorem says that convolving with $G_t$ in real space is multiplying by
$\hat G_t(k) = e^{-\nu k^2 t}$ in Fourier space. Each picture makes a
different property obvious:

* **Fourier**: the dynamics is *diagonal*. Modes never talk to each other.
  Decay rates are read off instantly. Semi-group property
  $e^{-\nu k^2 t_1} e^{-\nu k^2 t_2} = e^{-\nu k^2 (t_1+t_2)}$ is trivial.
* **Real space**: the dynamics is *local*. Information spreads a distance
  $\sqrt{\nu t}$; positivity is manifest ($G_t > 0$, so $\psi_0 \ge 0$ implies
  $\psi \ge 0$); the maximum principle holds.

Being able to switch between the two at will is the central skill of these
notes, and it is exactly what the Hopf–Cole transform will buy us for a
*nonlinear* equation.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it"}
Pick a rough initial condition (the step or the noise) and advance time. The
left panel shows $\psi(x,t)$ with the kernel $G_t$ drawn at the same scale;
the right panel shows $|\hat\psi_k|$ with the multiplier $e^{-\nu k^2 t}$. The
widths of the two curves are inverse to each other: $\sigma_x \sigma_k \sim 1$.
:::

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-cap: "A square pulse diffusing. Left: real space; the dashed curve is the heat kernel at the latest time. Right: Fourier amplitudes; the dashed curve is the multiplier exp(−νk²t)."
#| label: fig-heat
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
L, N, nu = 2.0, 512, 0.002
x = np.arange(-L/2, L/2, L/N); k = 2*np.pi*np.fft.fftfreq(N, d=L/N)
psi0 = (np.abs(x) < 0.25).astype(float)
times = [0, 0.5, 2, 8]
fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4))
for t in times:
    psi = np.fft.ifft(np.fft.fft(psi0)*np.exp(-nu*k**2*t)).real
    a1.plot(x, psi, label=f"t = {t}")
    kk = np.fft.fftshift(k); a2.semilogy(kk, np.abs(np.fft.fftshift(np.fft.fft(psi)))/N + 1e-16, label=f"t = {t}")
G = np.exp(-x**2/(4*nu*times[-1]))/np.sqrt(4*np.pi*nu*times[-1])
a1.plot(x, G*0.5/G.max(), "k--", lw=1, label="heat kernel (scaled)")
a2.semilogy(kk, np.exp(-nu*kk**2*times[-1])*0.25, "k--", lw=1, label=r"$e^{-\nu k^2 t}$ (scaled)")
a1.set_xlabel("x"); a1.set_ylabel(r"$\psi$"); a1.legend(fontsize=8)
a2.set_xlabel("k"); a2.set_ylabel(r"$|\hat\psi_k|$"); a2.set_xlim(-200, 200); a2.set_ylim(1e-7, 1); a2.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
```

## Why linearity is everything

Try to repeat the Fourier argument for Burgers' equation. The term $u u_x$
becomes, in Fourier space,

$$
\widehat{(u u_x)}_k = \frac{i}{2}\sum_{p+q=k} q\,\hat u_p\,\hat u_q ,
$$ {#eq-burgers-conv}

a **convolution**: mode $k$ is fed by all pairs $(p, q)$ with $p + q = k$. The
modes are coupled, energy cascades from large to small scales, and we are
back to time stepping. This mode-mode coupling is not a nuisance to be
eliminated; it is the physics of shocks and, later, of the cosmic web. The
remarkable fact of the next chapter is that a clever change of variable
*moves all of the coupling into a single nonlinear transformation* applied
before and after a purely linear evolution.
